lines.trans: Salma! Look at you standing at the stove on both feet!
Two days on those pillows worked miracles—not a single twinge today!
Good thing too, Chef, because we brought forty fresh lemons from the market.
Forty lemons means four big trays of almond lemon tart for six o'clock!
How many neighbours do you think will actually come tonight, Salma?
Word travels fast on Jasmine Street when free music and warm bread meet!
I already sliced ten lemons; Nour is beating the eggs and sugar.
Did you check the big red label on the sugar jar first, Nour?
Checked twice AND tasted a pinch! Sweet as summer!
What about hot tea for twenty-four cups at once, Salma?
Two big pots of black tea, two pots of fresh courtyard mint, and hot milk.
Into the oven goes tray number one—six o'clock, here we come!

meanings.note: Color adjective with feminine حمرا (hamra); شاي أحمر means black tea.

examples.trans: Would you like coffee or black tea?
There is a red ribbon on my suitcase.

meanings.note: The number four, used with masculine nouns.

examples.trans: Room four is arriving today.
Four tables and eight chairs in the courtyard.

meanings.note: Numeral 'forty'.

examples.trans: The bus arrives in forty minutes.
I do not wear size forty-four!

meanings.note: First person singular pronoun.

examples.trans: I am Nour, the new receptionist.
I am Salma from the kitchen.

meanings.note: Before an indefinite noun أول means 'first' (أول يوم 'first day'); after a definite noun الأول / الأولى agrees in gender (الصفحة الأولى 'the first page'). Also used adverbially ('first').

examples.trans: Welcome on your first day of work!
Read the first page calmly.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian masculine noun. Plural: أباريق.

examples.trans: The teapot is hot on the table.
Pour the hot water into the teapot.

meanings.note: Core Jordanian everyday verb for 'to come' (إجا / بيجي).

examples.trans: You came ten minutes early.
I will come on Friday at noon.

meanings.note: Spoken Jordanian pronoun for 'we' (equivalent to formal نحن).

examples.trans: We respect all our guests.
We are ready for breakfast.

meanings.note: Feminine verb form meaning 'to gather' or 'come together'.

examples.text: العيلة كلها اجتمعت عالغدا يوم الجمعة.
examples.trans: The whole family gathered for lunch on Friday.

examples.text: بكرا رح نجتمع بالمكتب عشان نرتب الخطة.
examples.trans: Tomorrow we'll meet at the office to organize the plan.

meanings.note: Common Arabic verb meaning 'to spread', with the spoken Levantine b- prefix.

examples.text: ريحة القهوة المحمّصة بتنتشر بكل الحارة الصبح.
examples.trans: The aroma of roasted coffee spreads through the whole neighborhood in the morning.
The news spread quickly among the neighbors.

meanings.note: Collective plural بيض ('eggs'), singulative بيضة ('one egg'), dual بيضتين ('two eggs').

examples.trans: I fried two eggs for breakfast.
Hot eggs are delicious with bread.

meanings.note: Past tense Arabic verb meaning 'to make sure' or 'verify', conjugated for a woman.

examples.text: تأكدتي إنو الباب تسكّر منيح قبل ما تطلعي؟
examples.trans: Did you make sure the door was locked properly before you left?

examples.text: لازم نتأكد من الموعد قبل ما نحجز التذاكر.
examples.trans: We need to verify the appointment before booking the tickets.

meanings.note: Baked fruit or custard tart, especially تارت الليمون ('lemon tart').

examples.text: تارت الليمون بقشرة اللوز طلع أطيب واحد.
examples.trans: The lemon tart with the almond crust turned out to be the tastiest one.

examples.text: خلينا قطعة تارت صغيرة لطارق بالمطبخ.
examples.trans: We saved a small slice of tart for Tariq in the kitchen.

meanings.note: Form II verbal noun of قطّع (to chop into pieces); لوح تقطيع is a cutting board.

examples.text: تقطيع البندورة والخيار بياخد عشر دقايق بس.
examples.trans: Chopping the tomatoes and cucumbers only takes ten minutes.

examples.text: لوح التقطيع الخشبي محطوط جنب المجلى.
examples.trans: The wooden cutting board is placed next to the sink.

meanings.note: The number 2.

examples.trans: He has two left on the shelf.
Hold the torch, the two of you!

meanings.note: Common Levantine Arabic verb meaning 'to expect', with feminine ending -i.

examples.trans: Do you think it's going to rain tomorrow?

examples.text: ما توقّعت أبداً أشوفك هون اليوم!
examples.trans: I never expected to see you here today!

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian verb; spoken present adds the b- prefix (بجيب, بيجيب).

examples.text: رح أجيب شراشف نظيفة من الخزانة.
examples.trans: I will bring clean sheets from the closet.

examples.text: أي علبة زبدة جبتي يا نور؟
examples.trans: Which tub of butter did you bring, Nour?

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian masculine noun. Plural: جيران.

examples.trans: All the neighbours on the street are kind.
Good morning, dear neighbour.

meanings.note: Active participle of إجا ('to come'): means 'on the way / arriving' (جايين 'they are coming') and after a time noun 'next' (الأسبوع الجاي 'next week').

examples.trans: The guests are coming down the stairs now.
We will see you next week!

meanings.note: Extremely common Jordanian expression to express surprise or ask for confirmation, like 'really?' or 'seriously!'.

examples.trans: My grandfather's workshop was on this street.
Did you really finish all the work?

meanings.note: With possessive endings, حال acts as 'myself/yourself/itself' (لحاله by itself, لا تغلبي حالك don't tire yourself).

examples.trans: The door opened by itself from the wind.
How are you doing today?

meanings.note: One of the most frequently used adjectives in Jordanian Arabic to mean beautiful, sweet, nice, or good.

examples.trans: The strawberry jam is sweet and tasty.
The sweater looks lovely and warm.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian masculine noun.

examples.trans: I would like coffee with hot milk.
We bought three bottles of milk.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian masculine noun. Plural: أخبار.

examples.trans: I have good news for you today!
They have no news yet.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian masculine noun. Plural: خبزات.

examples.trans: The morning bread is fresh and hot.
We ate bread with cheese and olives.

meanings.note: Culinary verb for whisking eggs, lemon curd, or cream until smooth.

examples.text: نور بتخفق البيض مع الليمون والسكر بهدوء.
examples.trans: Nour whisks the eggs gently with lemon and sugar.

examples.text: خفقت سلمى الكريمة حتى صارت ناعمة ومتساوية.
examples.trans: Salma whisked the curd until it turned smooth and glossy.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian verb; spoken present adds the b- prefix (بخلص, بيخلص).

examples.trans: I finished making the bed quickly!

examples.text: كل ما أخلص عزف كنا نحكي.
examples.trans: Whenever I finished playing, we used to chat.

meanings.note: Used to describe warm weather, warm water, or a cozy feeling.

examples.trans: The bread is warm and fresh from the oven.
Sitting in the attic is cozy when it rains.

meanings.note: Spoken Levantine hollow verb (from Classical ذاق, with ذ -> د); imperative دوق / دوقي ('taste!').

examples.text: دوقي هالمربى الحلو قبل ما نشتري المرطبان.
examples.trans: Taste this sweet jam before we buy the jar.
Ziad tasted the honey and smiled right away.

meanings.note: Common everyday verb for 'went' in the past tense. Also used as a future particle.

examples.trans: We missed our chance — he hung up!

examples.text: كل التعب راح مع أول فنجان قهوة.
examples.trans: All the tiredness vanished with the first cup of coffee.

meanings.note: Feminine body-part noun in Levantine Arabic (رجلك اليمين 'your right foot').

examples.text: ارفعي رجلك عالمخدة وارتاحي نص ساعة.
examples.trans: Prop your foot up on the pillow and rest for half an hour.

examples.text: حطيت كيس تلج ملفوف بمنشفة على رجلي.
examples.trans: I placed an ice pack wrapped in a towel on my foot.

meanings.note: Instance noun from رش ('sprinkle/spray'): رشة ملح = 'a pinch of salt'.

examples.text: الشوربة بدها بس رشة ملح وعصرة ليمون.
examples.trans: The soup just needs a pinch of salt and a squeeze of lemon.

examples.text: حطي رشة قرفة ناعمة فوق الفنجان.
examples.trans: Put a light sprinkle of ground cinnamon on top of the cup.

meanings.note: Everyday word for a number, digit, or phone number.

examples.trans: Here is your key, room number four.
Is there a phone number written on the paper?

meanings.note: Extremely common Levantine preposition meaning 'like' or 'similar to'.

examples.trans: I want a glass of tea like yesterday.
Do it the way I taught you.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian feminine noun. Plural: ساحات.

examples.trans: The courtyard has a big jasmine tree.
We sat drinking tea in the courtyard.

meanings.note: Everyday word for an hour of time, a wristwatch, or a wall clock.

examples.trans: What time is it right now, please?
We arrived an hour ago on the dot.

meanings.note: The number 6.

examples.trans: Room six is on the second floor.
I have six lemons in the basket.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian adjective (feminine: سخنة, plural: سخنين).

examples.trans: Drink a glass of hot tea first.
Pour the hot water into the pot.

meanings.note: With ب- forms the very common adverb بسرعة ('quickly / fast').

examples.trans: I always walk fast in the morning.
Your quick wit saved the day!

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian masculine noun.

examples.trans: I like black tea without sugar.
We sprinkled powdered sugar over the cake.

meanings.note: Female given name belonging to the café's morning baker.

examples.text: سلمى بتخبز الكرواسون والخبز كل يوم الفجر.
examples.trans: Salma bakes the croissants and bread every day at dawn.

examples.text: سلمى جابت صينية كعك طازة للضيوف.
examples.trans: Salma brought a tray of fresh cookies for the guests.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian masculine noun. Plural: أسواق.

examples.text: سوق وسط البلد مليان حركة الصبح.
examples.trans: The downtown market is bustling in the morning.
We bought fresh herbs from the market.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian masculine noun. Plural: شوارع.

examples.trans: Our guesthouse is on a quiet street in central Amman.
There are old stone streets in the quarter.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian verb for 'to see, look, check' (بشوف / شاف).

examples.trans: Look inside the suitcase, Nour!
I will see you tomorrow at breakfast.

meanings.note: A staple beverage in Jordanian culture, typically served with mint or sage.

examples.trans: Please have a glass of hot mint tea.
There is black tea and coffee at breakfast.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian interrogative pronoun for 'what'.

examples.trans: What is that sound?
What is written on the sheet, Rami?

meanings.note: Used across modern Jordanian kitchens and cafés for both male and female head chefs.

examples.text: الدفتر جاهز يا شيف سلمى، بشو نبلش؟
examples.trans: The clipboard is ready, Chef Salma—what do we start with?

examples.text: الشيف ذاق الشوربة وابتسم من أول معلقة.
examples.trans: The chef tasted the soup and smiled from the very first spoonful.

meanings.note: The season of summer.

examples.trans: Evenings in Amman are pleasant in summer.
Our rent is paid until next summer.

meanings.note: Broken plural صواني ('serving trays' or 'oven baking pans').

examples.text: جهزنا تلات صواني خبز عشان تدخل الفرن الفجر.
examples.trans: We prepped three trays of bread to go into the oven at dawn.

examples.text: نور حملت صينية الشاي بالنعنع للساحة.
examples.trans: Nour carried the mint tea tray out to the courtyard.

meanings.note: Used for fresh food, produce, or bread.

examples.text: خبز سلمى طازة وسخن كل صبح.
examples.trans: Salma's bread is fresh and hot every morning.

examples.text: اشترينا ليمون طازة ونعنع أخضر من السوق.
examples.trans: We bought fresh lemons and green mint from the market.

meanings.note: The standalone number ten.

examples.trans: You arrived ten minutes early.
Breakfast is from seven-thirty to ten.

meanings.note: The number twenty.

examples.trans: We need twenty eggs for breakfast.
The ring's width is twenty millimetres.

meanings.note: Standard preposition for 'on', 'upon', or 'to'.

examples.trans: Your glasses are on your forehead!
Say hello to Salma for me!

meanings.note: Levantine progressive marker placed before a present-tense verb to show action happening right now.

examples.trans: The water is flowing inside the pipe right now!

examples.text: كنت عم بدور على دفتري هلا.
examples.trans: I was just looking for my notebook.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian verb; spoken present adds the b- prefix (بعمل, بيعمل).

examples.text: اليوم رح نعمل بيض عالطريقة الفرنسية!
examples.trans: Today we will make French-style eggs!
What do we do now with the rain coming down?

meanings.note: Means 'about' (عن الزبدة), 'off / away from' (عن جبيني), and appears in عن جد ('really!') and عن إذنك ('excuse me').

examples.trans: I will carry the suitcase up for you.
I heard your voices about the butter!

meanings.note: A very common preposition used to indicate location, possession, or presence.

examples.trans: A taxi just stopped at the door.
I have a reservation under the name Suad.

meanings.note: In Jordanian homes and kitchens, الغاز routinely means 'the kitchen stove / range'.

examples.text: حطيت طنجرة الشوربة عالغاز على نار هادية.
examples.trans: I set the soup pot on the stove over a gentle flame.

examples.text: طفي الغاز لما يصفر المؤقت بعد عشر دقايق.
examples.trans: Turn off the stove when the timer rings in ten minutes.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian masculine noun. Plural: أفران.

examples.text: لفائف القرفة طلعت من الفرن هلا.
examples.trans: The cinnamon rolls just came out of the oven.
The bakery down the street bakes in the morning.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian masculine noun. Plural: فناجين.

examples.trans: I set two teacups on the tray.
This is my favourite coffee cup.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian word for soon or near.

examples.text: علمت بيانو ببيت قريب من هون.
examples.trans: I taught piano in a house near here.
We booked a table at a nearby restaurant.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian adjective (feminine: كبيرة, plural: كبار).

examples.trans: We use this big paper ledger.
You know older brothers well!

meanings.note: Placed AFTER the adjective or verb it intensifies: تقيلة كتير ('very heavy'), شكرا كتير ('thank you very much').

examples.trans: The smell is so good!
This suitcase is very heavy today.

meanings.note: In questions كم + singular noun asks 'how many?'; in statements كم + singular noun means 'a few' (كم دقيقة 'a few minutes').

examples.trans: Give him a few minutes, Rami.

examples.text: كم لفة قرفة بيقدر فرنك يخبز؟
examples.trans: How many cinnamon rolls can your oven bake?

meanings.note: Indispensable Levantine and Egyptian particle meaning 'also', 'too', or 'as well'.

examples.text: التفكير السريع أنقذ الفطور كمان مرة!
examples.trans: Quick thinking saved breakfast once again!
And I missed you too.

meanings.note: Takes pronoun suffixes in spoken Jordanian: لأني (because I), لأنك (because you), لأنه (because he/it — also general 'because'), لأنكم (because you pl.).

examples.text: لأنه القهوة الطيبة بتخلي الناس لطاف!
examples.trans: Because good coffee makes people pleasant!
Thank you because you kept the bag safe.

meanings.note: Common conjunction used to introduce a time clause, distinct from the question word 'when' (mita).

examples.trans: Smile when the bell rings!
When I get nervous, my sentences turn long.

meanings.note: Literally means almonds, but heavily used in Jordanian youth slang to mean 'everything is perfect' or 'great'.

examples.text: ريحة اللوز المحمص طالعة من فرن سلمى.
examples.trans: The aroma of toasted almonds is drifting out of Salma's oven.

examples.text: قشرة اللوز بتعطي تارت الليمون قرمشة طيبة.
examples.trans: An almond crust gives the lemon tart a delicious crunch.

meanings.note: Definite الليلة means 'tonight', while indefinite ليلة means 'one night / night of'.

examples.trans: I am going to sleep well tonight.
We booked the room for three nights.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian masculine noun. Plural: ليمون.

examples.trans: The warm lemon cake is ready.
I squeezed half a lemon into the soup.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian adjective (feminine: مجانية, plural: —).

examples.text: فطور مجاني طول الأسبوع مع الغرفة!
examples.trans: Complimentary breakfast all week with the room!
Morning coffee is free for the neighbours today.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian feminine noun. Plural: مخدات.

examples.trans: I put two soft pillows on the bed.
The cotton pillow is comfortable for sleeping.

meanings.note: 'Marrah' means 'a time/once' (e.g. waḥdeh marrah = one time), but 'mara' (مَرَة) means 'woman/wife' in colloquial Jordanian.

examples.trans: The doorbell rang twice.
I read the letter three times.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian word for a glass jam, honey, or olive jar (dual مرطبانين, plural مرطبانات).

examples.trans: We lined the jars of jam and honey up on the shelf.
Open the new jar of honey for breakfast.

meanings.note: Feminine plural of معجزة, meaning 'miracles'.

examples.text: إنو لحقنا الطيارة بآخر لحظة كان عنجد معجزة!
examples.trans: That we caught the plane at the very last second was honestly a miracle!

examples.text: ستي دايماً بتحكي الصبر والعمل بسوّوا معجزات.
examples.trans: My grandma always says patience and hard work work miracles.

meanings.note: Dual ملصقين ('the two labels'), plural ملصقات ('labels / stickers').

examples.text: نور كتبت ملصقات واضحة وكبيرة لكل المرتبانات.
examples.trans: Nour wrote big, clear labels for all the jars.

examples.text: تأكد إن الملصقين ناشفين قبل ما تمسك القزاز.
examples.trans: Make sure both labels are dry before you pick up the glass.

meanings.note: One of the most basic Arabic prepositions indicating origin.

examples.trans: I am Salma from the kitchen.
Breakfast is from seven-thirty to ten.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian word for 'good' and adverbially 'well' (نمت منيح؟ 'did you sleep well?').

examples.trans: It has a good, comfortable wooden bed.
Did you sleep well under the wooden ceiling?

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian feminine noun.

examples.trans: We found an old music book in the suitcase.
Gentle music is soothing in the evening.

meanings.note: In Levantine Arabic, a noun for a sharp twinge or sudden prick of pain.

examples.text: حسّيت بنخزة خفيفة بضهري لما رفعت الصندوق التقيل.
examples.trans: I felt a slight twinge in my back when I lifted the heavy box.

examples.text: نخزة الإبرة كانت سريعة وما وجعت أبداً.
examples.trans: The prick of the needle was quick and didn't hurt at all.

meanings.note: Common Arabic phrase بالنسبة لـ meaning 'as for' or 'what about'.

examples.text: بالنسبة للموعد بكرا، خلينا نتلاقى الساعة عشرة.
examples.trans: As for tomorrow's appointment, let's meet at ten o'clock.

examples.text: وبالنسبة للأكل، سلمى رح تجهز الفطاير.
examples.trans: And regarding the food, Salma will prepare the pastries.

meanings.note: A very common herb used in Levantine tea and cuisine.

examples.trans: Tea with fresh mint warms the heart.
We planted mint in the courtyard beside the tree.

meanings.note: Appears in صباح النور ('morning of light', the standard reply to صباح الخير) and نور الشمس ('sunlight').

examples.trans: Good morning and welcome!
We read the card in the sunlight.

meanings.note: Spoken Jordanian presentative word ('here is! / look!') pointing to someone or something right now; takes suffixes (هيهم hayy-hum 'here they are!').

examples.text: هي تاكسي وقف عند الباب هلا!
examples.trans: Look, a taxi just stopped at the door!
Here they come down the stairs!

meanings.note: Cardinal number or used as an indefinite pronoun.

examples.trans: Not a single scratch on the cup!
The gate rang with one strong ring.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian adjective (feminine: واقفة, plural: واقفين).

examples.trans: There is nobody standing in the courtyard.
They stood face to face under the tree.

meanings.note: Used in negative constructions or as a strong negative emphasis.

examples.trans: Is the window facing the street or the courtyard?
Not a single drop of water on the table!

meanings.note: Vocative particle used when addressing someone directly.

examples.trans: Good morning, Tariq!
Oh, how lovely the sun is after the rain!

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian masculine noun. Plural: ياسمين.

examples.trans: The jasmine vine climbs above the door.
The evening scent of jasmine lifts the spirit.

meanings.note: Everyday conversational bridge introducing an inference ('so that means...'), clarification, or gentle pause ('I mean...').

examples.trans: So the house says hello by itself?
Does that mean there is no heating tonight?

meanings.note: Standard noun for day, often used in expressions like 'el-yom' (today).

examples.trans: Today the weather is sunny and warm in Amman.
Have a happy, successful day!
